idea.body: Sometimes the outcomes you want are hard to count directly, but the ones you do not want are easy. Count the whole set, count the ones you do not want, and subtract: total minus not wanted equals wanted. A rover's toolkit has 20 parts, and 3 are damaged. Instead of counting the 17 good parts one at a time, subtract: 20 minus 3 is 17. The trick pays off most on questions with the word at least, like at least one match rolling two dice. Counting every way to avoid a match is one clean case, while counting every way to get a match directly means checking many cases.

figure.alt: A box for all outcomes, minus a box for the ones not wanted, equals a box for the ones wanted.

workedExample.prompt: Two dice are rolled. In how many of the 36 outcomes does at least one die show a 6?
steps: There are 6 times 6, or 36, total outcomes for two dice.
Counting every way to get at least one 6 directly means checking several overlapping cases.
It is easier to count the outcomes with no 6 at all: 5 choices for each die, so 5 times 5 is 25.
The outcomes with at least one 6 are the rest: 36 minus 25 is 11.

ways.name: Total minus not wanted
ways.when: Use this when you already know the total and the count you do not want.
steps: A 3D print farm has 45 jobs queued in total.
8 of them are rush jobs, the ones not wanted here.
ways.example: A 3D print farm has 45 jobs queued. 8 are rush jobs. How many are not rush jobs?
ways.trap: Adding the two counts together instead of subtracting.

figure.alt: A box for total 45 minus rush 8 equals not rush 37.

ways.name: None at all, then subtract
ways.when: Use this when at least one of something is hard to count directly.
steps: A 3-digit code uses digits 0 to 9, repeats allowed, so there are 1000 codes in all.
Codes with no 7 anywhere use only 9 choices per digit: 9 times 9 times 9 is 729.
271 codes have at least one digit equal to 7.
ways.example: A 3-digit code uses digits 0 to 9, repeats allowed. How many codes have at least one 7?
ways.trap: Counting only codes that start with 7, missing the ones with a 7 in another spot.

ways.name: Neither condition, by overlap
ways.when: Use this when neither of two conditions is easier to count directly than at least one of them.
steps: Count the whole numbers from 1 to 60 divisible by 4: 15 of them.
Count the ones divisible by 6: 10 of them.
Numbers divisible by both 4 and 6 are divisible by 12, their shared multiple: 5 of them, counted twice above.
Divisible by 4 or 6 is 15 plus 10 minus 5, which is 20.
ways.example: How many whole numbers from 1 to 60 are divisible by neither 4 nor 6?
ways.trap: Adding the two counts without subtracting the overlap, double counting the shared multiples.

bank.prompt: The wanted count and the not-wanted count always add up to the total.
explanation: Take a bag of 20 marbles where 6 are wanted and 14 are not.
6 plus 14 is 20, the whole bag.
Every marble is either wanted or not wanted, never both, so the two counts always add back to the total.
bank.useAgain: when you need to reason about how a total splits between wanted and not wanted.
hints: Try the statement on a small, concrete total and part.
The wanted count and the not-wanted count always add back up to the total.
bank.socraticHint: Does the wanted count plus the not-wanted count always equal the whole total?

bank.prompt: Complementary counting only works when the not-wanted count is bigger than the wanted count.
explanation: Take a bag of 20 marbles where 15 are wanted and only 5 are not wanted.
Here the not-wanted count, 5, is smaller than the wanted count, not bigger.
Subtracting the not-wanted count from the total still gives the correct wanted count, no matter which count is bigger.
bank.useAgain: when you need to reason about how a total splits between wanted and not wanted.
hints: Try the statement on a small, concrete total and part.

bank.socraticHint: Does the wanted count plus the not-wanted count always equal the whole total?

bank.prompt: If you already know the total and the not-wanted count, subtracting gives the wanted count.
explanation: Take a bag of 20 marbles where 5 are not wanted.
20 minus 5 is 15, the wanted count.
That subtraction always works, since the wanted and not-wanted counts together make up the whole total.
bank.useAgain: when you need to reason about how a total splits between wanted and not wanted.
